screens.title: Value vs Reference Types
screens.narratorSegment: A fundamental design choice in Swift is whether a type is a value type or a reference type. Value types, like structs and enums, copy on assignment or when passed into functions. That means each variable holds its own independent data. The chapter example of a Coordinate struct shows altering a copy does not affect the original. In contrast, classes are reference types. When you assign a class instance, you're copying a pointer to the same memory. Changes through any reference are visible to all references. The UserAccount example in the source demonstrates how modifying a balance through one variable affects the other because they refer to the same object. Practically, pick structs for small, immutable-like data models — points, colors, simple state snapshots — where independent copies are expected. Pick classes for objects that must share identity or mutable state across parts of an app, such as a session manager or network client. A common misconception is that performance alone should drive the choice. Instead, prioritize semantics: do you need identity and shared, mutable state? If not, prefer value semantics to avoid surprising shared mutations. To check your understanding, imagine copying a player score struct versus sharing a player profile object — which should be a struct and which should be a class, and why?

keyIdea.title: Value vs Reference
keyIdea.text: Use structs for independent copies and classes for shared identity; the difference prevents or enables shared mutations.

content.html:
Core Concept

Value vs Reference Types

Understand copying semantics and design types that behave predictably.

Struct (Value Type)
struct Coordinate {
  var x: Double
  var y: Double
}

var location1 = Coordinate(x: 10.0, y: 20.0)
var location2 = location1 // copy
location2.x = 30.0

// location1 remains unchanged
Good for points, colors, small models where separate copies are safer.
Class (Reference Type)
class UserAccount {
  var username: String
  var balance: Double
  init(username: String, balance: Double) { self.username = username; self.balance = balance }
}

var account1 = UserAccount(username: "Alice", balance: 100.0)
var account2 = account1 // reference
account2.balance += 50.0
// account1.balance is now 150.0
Use classes when a single shared instance should reflect changes across the app.
Example
Coordinate copy vs UserAccount shared balance illustrates the difference clearly.
Common Mistake
Using a class for simple data containers introduces unintended shared mutations.
Key Takeaway
Prefer value types for isolated data, classes for identity and shared mutable state.

screens.title: Structs, Methods, and Mutating
screens.narratorSegment: Structs are value types and therefore copy when assigned. When a method on a struct needs to change its stored properties, Swift requires the method to be marked mutating. This signals that the method will replace or modify the value instance, which is important because otherwise a struct's methods are treated as read-only on copies. A concrete example from the chapter shows a User struct conforming to a protocol where logout is mutating because it updates isLoggedIn. Practically, use mutating only when necessary: prefer creating new immutable instances where possible, but mark methods mutating when state changes are natural and efficient. A common misconception is that mutating means the method will change other references; it does not, because each struct method operates on its own copy. Also note that classes never require mutating because they are reference types and methods can change properties directly. When designing APIs, be explicit: if a struct presents behaviors that change state, document and mark them mutating, and consider whether a class's shared identity might better capture intent if multiple parts of your app must observe the same instance changes.

keyIdea.title: Mutating methods
keyIdea.text: Mark struct methods mutating when they modify stored properties; this preserves value-type semantics and clarity.

content.html:
Definition

Structs, Methods, and Mutating

Why the mutating keyword exists and how it preserves value semantics.

Protocol Example
protocol Authenticatable {
  var email: String { get }
  func login(password: String) -> Bool
  mutating func logout()
}

struct User: Authenticatable {
  let email: String
  var isLoggedIn: Bool = false

  func login(password: String) -> Bool { /* ... */ }
  mutating func logout() { isLoggedIn = false }
}
Because User is a struct, logout must be mutating to change isLoggedIn.
Contrast: Classes
Classes do not require mutating. Instance methods can modify stored properties directly because references point to the same object.
Practical Tip
Choose structs for small, copyable models; choose classes if shared identity and observation are needed.
Example
A user session may be a class; a display coordinate should be a struct.
Misconception
Mutating does not change other copies; it changes only that struct instance.
Check
If multiple references must reflect the same state, prefer a class over a struct.

screens.title: Classes, Inheritance, and Overriding
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance in Swift is provided only by classes. It lets a subclass inherit properties and methods from a superclass, creating an is-a relationship. The chapter example defines an Animal superclass with a generic makeSound method, then a Dog subclass that adds a breed property, calls super. init in its initializer, and overrides makeSound to provide a specialized behavior. Subclasses can also add new methods, such as fetch. When overriding, use override to make intent explicit. Use final on classes or methods to prevent further subclassing or overriding if you want to preserve a stable implementation and allow compiler optimizations. A common pitfall is deep, rigid inheritance hierarchies that become difficult to maintain. Prefer composition — building types by containing other types — when behavior can be assembled without forcing an is-a relationship. In practice, design shallow inheritance trees with clear responsibilities: a superclass provides shared behavior, and subclasses extend or refine that behavior. A quick check: if two types share behavior but not identity, consider a protocol and composition instead of inheritance. Classes, Inheritance, and Overriding means use small, focused class hierarchies; override explicitly and avoid deep inheritance by favoring composition when possible.. In practical terms, create hierarchies and specialize behavior with subclasses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow

Classes, Inheritance, and Overriding

How to extend behavior through subclassing safely.

Superclass: Animal
class Animal {
  var name: String
  init(name: String) { self.name = name }
  func makeSound() { print("Generic animal sound") }
}
Subclass: Dog
class Dog: Animal {
  var breed: String
  init(name: String, breed: String) {
    self.breed = breed
    super.init(name: name)
  }
  override func makeSound() { print("Woof!") }
  func fetch() { print("\(name) is fetching.") }
}
Example
Dog inherits name and makeSound, then overrides to specialize behavior.
Pitfall
Deep inheritance can make changes fragile; prefer composition when possible.
Check
If you need single shared identity and specialized behavior, subclassing can be appropriate.

screens.title: Protocols and Polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: Protocols provide a blueprint of properties and methods that any type — class, struct, or enum — can conform to. They enable polymorphism by letting you write code that expects a protocol rather than a specific concrete type. The chapter's Authenticatable example shows a protocol declaring an email property, a login method, and a mutating logout method. A struct or a class can conform and implement these requirements differently. Unlike inheritance, a type can conform to multiple protocols, which makes them ideal for composing capabilities such as Persistable, Drivable, or Transactable. Protocols shine when different types need to present the same A P I: for example, both a User class and an Admin struct could conform to Authenticatable and be handled by the same authentication flow. A common misconception is thinking protocols implement behavior; they declare requirements. Default implementations can be provided via protocol extensions, but the protocol itself is a contract. When designing your app, prefer protocols to define roles and behaviors, and use them together with concrete types to keep code loosely coupled and testable. Protocols and Polymorphism means define behavior contracts that multiple, diverse types can adopt to enable polymorphism without inheritance.. In practical terms, protocols define contracts; types conform to show the same behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison

Protocols and Polymorphism

Contracts make code flexible and testable across types.

Protocol Definition
protocol Authenticatable {
  var email: String { get }
  func login(password: String) -> Bool
  mutating func logout()
}
This declares expectations for conforming types without prescribing how they implement them.
Conformance Example
struct User: Authenticatable {
  let email: String
  var isLoggedIn: Bool = false
  func login(password: String) -> Bool { /* ... */ }
  mutating func logout() { isLoggedIn = false }
}
Both structs and classes can conform and be used via the protocol type.
Use Case
Define a Persistable or Transactable protocol and implement it across varied account types.
Misconception
Protocols do not supply behavior unless you use protocol extensions to add defaults.
Check
Can two unrelated types implement the same protocol? Yes — that's polymorphism.

screens.title: Access Control in Swift
screens.narratorSegment: Access control helps you declare who can see and use your types, properties, and methods. Swift provides five levels: private, fileprivate, internal (the default), public, and open. Private restricts access to the enclosing declaration, while fileprivate allows access across the same source file. Internal is visible within the same module and is sufficient for most app-internal code. Public exposes an A P I, and open allows subclassing and overriding outside the defining module. Use private to hide helper methods that others shouldn't depend on, and use internal for typical app code. Public and open are for reusable frameworks where you must be deliberate about what you expose. Encapsulation works hand-in-hand with access control: by keeping implementation private, you present a smaller, more stable surface for other code to rely upon. A common misconception is using public by default; instead default to internal and increase visibility only when necessary. As a practical tip, mark properties private when external components should not mutate them directly and provide controlled methods to interact with state. Access Control in Swift means choose the narrowest access level that still allows needed interactions; prefer private/internal to protect implementation.. In practical terms, managing visibility to protect implementation details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Access Control

Keep internal details hidden and expose a stable interface.

private / fileprivate
Hide implementation inside a declaration or file. Use for helper methods and internal state you don't want others to call.
internal
Default for app modules. Accessible throughout your target and appropriate for most code.
public / open
Use when exposing APIs from frameworks. Open additionally allows external subclassing and overriding.
Example
Mark internal helper methods private to keep a clean public API for a BankAccount class.
Misconception
Avoid defaulting to public for convenience — it increases your maintenance burden.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Designing a BankAccount Class

Implement methods to protect invariants like non-negative balances.

Starter Code
class BankAccount {
  let accountNumber: String
  var accountHolder: String
  var balance: Double

  init(accountNumber: String, accountHolder: String, balance: Double) {
    self.accountNumber = accountNumber
    self.accountHolder = accountHolder
    self.balance = balance
  }

  func deposit(amount: Double) {
    // implement: increase balance and print message
  }

  func withdraw(amount: Double) {
    // implement: prevent balance < 0 and print message
  }
}
Design Notes
  • Keep balance private to the class by providing controlled methods.
  • Validate withdraw amounts to maintain invariants.
  • Print informative messages for each transaction for debugging and tests.
Check
After implementing, test deposit and withdraw to confirm balance updates and rejection on insufficient funds.

screens.title: PremiumAccount: Subclass and Overdraft
screens.narratorSegment: The PremiumAccount subclass extends BankAccount with an overdraftLimit and custom withdraw and applyInterest behavior. In the chapter task, PremiumAccount's withdraw should allow the balance to go negative up to the overdraft limit. That means your override must check amount against balance plus overdraftLimit and, if permitted, subtract the amount and print an appropriate message. The applyInterest method increases balance by a rate only if the balance is positive. This demonstrates specialization: PremiumAccount reuses BankAccount's core behavior and then refines rules to support premium customers. Remember to call super. init in the subclass initializer to set inherited properties. A typical mistake is duplicating logic already in the superclass rather than calling or extending it; prefer to reuse and then add checks. Also consider using final if you don't want further subclasses. As a design question, think about whether overdraft behavior belongs in a subclass or as a composed OverdraftPolicy object; composition can make behavior more flexible and testable. PremiumAccount: Subclass and Overdraft means override withdraw to honor overdraft limits and add applyinterest that acts only on positive balances.. In practical terms, extend bankaccount to allow overdraft and interest. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Architecture

PremiumAccount: Subclass and Overdraft

Extend behavior through subclassing with clear rules for overdraft and interest.

Subclass Starter
class PremiumAccount: BankAccount {
  var overdraftLimit: Double

  init(accountNumber: String, accountHolder: String, balance: Double, overdraftLimit: Double) {
    self.overdraftLimit = overdraftLimit
    super.init(accountNumber: accountNumber, accountHolder: accountHolder, balance: balance)
  }

  override func withdraw(amount: Double) {
    // allow balance to drop to -overdraftLimit
  }

  func applyInterest(rate: Double) {
    // increase balance by rate only if balance > 0
  }
}
Behavior Notes
  • Override withdraw to allow overdraft but still enforce a limit.
  • Apply interest only to positive balances to avoid rewarding negative balances.
  • Consider composition for flexible overdraft policies instead of subclassing.

Would an OverdraftPolicy object make testing and variation easier than subclassing? Consider it.

Process Flow

Transactable Protocol & Transfer Logic

A small transfer contract enforces safe fund movement between accounts.

Protocol
protocol Transactable {
  func transfer(amount: Double, to destinationAccount: BankAccount)
}
Both BankAccount and PremiumAccount will conform and implement transfer.
Implementation Notes
  • Try withdraw first and only deposit if it succeeds to avoid inconsistent state.
  • Respect the concrete rules of the source account (standard or premium) during withdraw.
  • Print messages describing the transaction success or failure for testing.
Example Test
Transfer 150 from Alice (BankAccount) to Bob (PremiumAccount) and verify both balances after operation.
Misconception
Don't deposit before confirming withdrawal success; this can leave destination funded without source deduction.
Check
Simulate scenarios including overdraft to ensure transfer semantics hold for all account types.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll learn how Swift expresses core object-oriented ideas using classes, structs, and protocols. You will see why choosing a class or a struct matters — because classes are reference types and structs are value types — and how that choice affects shared state, copying, and mutation in your app. We'll practice inheritance with subclassing and method overriding so you can create specialized types, and we'll use protocols to define contracts that different types can adopt. You'll also learn access control levels to protect implementation details and how to use properties and methods to encapsulate behavior. A practical task models a simple banking system so you can apply deposit, withdraw, transfer, and overdraft logic. Throughout, we'll highlight common mistakes, like overusing inheritance when composition is better, or using a class where a struct would avoid accidental shared state. By the end you'll be able to pick the right Swift type for a task, define clear protocols, and control visibility to write safer, modular iOS code. Ready to explore these building blocks and why they matter in real apps?

By the end of these lessons you will differentiate classes and structs, implement inheritance, define and conform to protocols, and apply access control to manage visibility. First, you'll learn the practical difference between value and reference types with concrete examples so you can choose the right container for data models. Second, you'll practice creating subclasses and overriding methods to specialize behavior and learn when to prefer composition over deep inheritance. Third, you'll design and use protocols to declare required methods and properties, which lets you write code that works across diverse types. Fourth, you'll use Swift's access control keywords to encapsulate implementation details so other parts of your app cannot accidentally rely on internal logic. Each objective includes hands-on examples and short checks to confirm understanding. These skills are essential for building maintainable, testable iOS code and for avoiding common bugs like unintended shared state or fragile inheritance trees.

These practice objectives guide how you will apply the chapter knowledge. You'll implement properties and methods to encapsulate behavior, including marking struct methods mutating when they change internal state. You'll design protocol blueprints and make types conform so you can write polymorphic code that handles different concrete types uniformly. You'll write a small banking example where a base BankAccount class implements deposit and withdraw, a PremiumAccount subclass adds overdraft behavior and interest, and both conform to a Transactable protocol for transfers. Each practice step reinforces a design decision: why a class suits a shared account instance, why an overdraft may allow negative balance, or why a struct would need mutating methods. Finally, you'll evaluate access control to protect helper methods used only within a file or type. These applied exercises help you see not only how the features work, but why you pick them in real app design.

A fundamental design choice in Swift is whether a type is a value type or a reference type. Value types, like structs and enums, copy on assignment or when passed into functions. That means each variable holds its own independent data. The chapter example of a Coordinate struct shows altering a copy does not affect the original. In contrast, classes are reference types. When you assign a class instance, you're copying a pointer to the same memory. Changes through any reference are visible to all references. The UserAccount example in the source demonstrates how modifying a balance through one variable affects the other because they refer to the same object. Practically, pick structs for small, immutable-like data models — points, colors, simple state snapshots — where independent copies are expected. Pick classes for objects that must share identity or mutable state across parts of an app, such as a session manager or network client. A common misconception is that performance alone should drive the choice. Instead, prioritize semantics: do you need identity and shared, mutable state? If not, prefer value semantics to avoid surprising shared mutations. To check your understanding, imagine copying a player score struct versus sharing a player profile object — which should be a struct and which should be a class, and why?

Structs are value types and therefore copy when assigned. When a method on a struct needs to change its stored properties, Swift requires the method to be marked mutating. This signals that the method will replace or modify the value instance, which is important because otherwise a struct's methods are treated as read-only on copies. A concrete example from the chapter shows a User struct conforming to a protocol where logout is mutating because it updates isLoggedIn. Practically, use mutating only when necessary: prefer creating new immutable instances where possible, but mark methods mutating when state changes are natural and efficient. A common misconception is that mutating means the method will change other references; it does not, because each struct method operates on its own copy. Also note that classes never require mutating because they are reference types and methods can change properties directly. When designing APIs, be explicit: if a struct presents behaviors that change state, document and mark them mutating, and consider whether a class's shared identity might better capture intent if multiple parts of your app must observe the same instance changes.

Inheritance in Swift is provided only by classes. It lets a subclass inherit properties and methods from a superclass, creating an is-a relationship. The chapter example defines an Animal superclass with a generic makeSound method, then a Dog subclass that adds a breed property, calls super. init in its initializer, and overrides makeSound to provide a specialized behavior. Subclasses can also add new methods, such as fetch. When overriding, use override to make intent explicit. Use final on classes or methods to prevent further subclassing or overriding if you want to preserve a stable implementation and allow compiler optimizations. A common pitfall is deep, rigid inheritance hierarchies that become difficult to maintain. Prefer composition — building types by containing other types — when behavior can be assembled without forcing an is-a relationship. In practice, design shallow inheritance trees with clear responsibilities: a superclass provides shared behavior, and subclasses extend or refine that behavior. A quick check: if two types share behavior but not identity, consider a protocol and composition instead of inheritance. Classes, Inheritance, and Overriding means use small, focused class hierarchies; override explicitly and avoid deep inheritance by favoring composition when possible.. In practical terms, create hierarchies and specialize behavior with subclasses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Protocols provide a blueprint of properties and methods that any type — class, struct, or enum — can conform to. They enable polymorphism by letting you write code that expects a protocol rather than a specific concrete type. The chapter's Authenticatable example shows a protocol declaring an email property, a login method, and a mutating logout method. A struct or a class can conform and implement these requirements differently. Unlike inheritance, a type can conform to multiple protocols, which makes them ideal for composing capabilities such as Persistable, Drivable, or Transactable. Protocols shine when different types need to present the same A P I: for example, both a User class and an Admin struct could conform to Authenticatable and be handled by the same authentication flow. A common misconception is thinking protocols implement behavior; they declare requirements. Default implementations can be provided via protocol extensions, but the protocol itself is a contract. When designing your app, prefer protocols to define roles and behaviors, and use them together with concrete types to keep code loosely coupled and testable. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Access control helps you declare who can see and use your types, properties, and methods. Swift provides five levels: private, fileprivate, internal (the default), public, and open. Private restricts access to the enclosing declaration, while fileprivate allows access across the same source file. Internal is visible within the same module and is sufficient for most app-internal code. Public exposes an A P I, and open allows subclassing and overriding outside the defining module. Use private to hide helper methods that others shouldn't depend on, and use internal for typical app code. Public and open are for reusable frameworks where you must be deliberate about what you expose. Encapsulation works hand-in-hand with access control: by keeping implementation private, you present a smaller, more stable surface for other code to rely upon. A common misconception is using public by default; instead default to internal and increase visibility only when necessary. As a practical tip, mark properties private when external components should not mutate them directly and provide controlled methods to interact with state.
